column3: Near-verbatim parallel: the messenger cannot guide the blind from error, but receptive believers hear and submit.
Directly pairs the blind with the messenger's inability to guide those who do not truly see.
Shows that conscious rejection after clear evidence is incompatible with divine guidance.
Directly joins making the deaf hear, guiding the blind, and manifest error.
The adjacent scene of mountains and divine craftsmanship does not clarify receptive guidance.
Connects submission, faith, and divine guidance, though without the hearing-blindness contrast.
Directly asks whether the deaf can be made to hear when they lack understanding.
The local punishment for evil deeds does not explain the limit on guiding the blind.
Explicitly contrasts offered guidance with preferring blindness over it.
Nearby denial of God's signs supplies the opposite response to the believers in 27:81.
Belief in revealed scripture exemplifies the receptive response named in 27:81.
Hearing guidance and then believing gives the positive sequence condensed in 27:81.
Sets belief in the revealed Book against rejection of God's signs.
Immediate antecedent: the messenger cannot make the dead or turning deaf hear the call.
Faith in God and His messenger culminating in submission parallels 27:81's receptive hearers.
Defines believers in the signs by their responsive, unarrogant reception of reminders.
Submission is shared, but this political command does not address hearing or guidance.
Directly combines belief in God's signs with being submitted.
Sustained submission is relevant, though the verse lacks the focus's reception imagery.
Those who hear the recitation believe and identify themselves as already submitted.
The greeting of peace has no material connection to blindness, hearing, or guidance.
The command to die submitted offers only broad background for the final word of 27:81.
Its signs for believers provide nearby support for the focus's believing recipients.
Forced surrender after false claims vanish contrasts with the willing submission of 27:81.
Absence of idle speech is unrelated to responsive hearing of revelation.
The description of the queen and her throne does not clarify the focus.
Names the Qur'an as guidance for believers, supporting the focus's positive recipient.
Directly says God makes whom He wills hear while the messenger cannot make graves hear.
Affirms that God guides whom He wills after sending clear signs.
Forbidden eavesdropping on the high assembly is a different kind of hearing.
Shows that nominal belief can be compromised by association, qualifying true belief.
The Qur'an's resolution of Israelite disputes is only broad local revelation context.
Commanded submission to God supplies a distant parallel to the focus's final term.
Hearing only a whisper on the Day of Judgment is not receptive hearing of guidance.
The believers' practices give broad local context but do not explain 27:81's contrast.
The call to submit to the one God gives a direct formulation of the focus's final response.
Belief in all revelation with humility illustrates genuine receptivity to divine signs.
The faithful are not deaf and blind when reminded of their Lord's signs.
Its statement that few believe offers only a general contrast to responsive believers.
Distinguishes personal guidance and error while limiting the messenger's role as guardian.
Immediate continuation calls the Qur'an guidance and mercy for believers.
Contrasts believing in a divine gift with turning people away from it.
Describes deniers of signs as deaf and dumb in darkness, with guidance under God's will.
Shows how embellished worship blocks people from the way so that they are not guided.
Faith and submission grow together in a tested response, though signs and hearing are absent.
Links guidance and misguidance to divine will within a communal test.
The hostile group's limited harm and defeat do not clarify the focus.
Material security from fear is not the faith or hearing of 27:81.
Combines faith in the revealed messages with explicit submission to God.
The nearby reward for good deeds gives outcome context but not the reception contrast.
States that God does not guide the defiantly corrupt, despite prophetic intercession.
The collective confession joins faith in revelation with being submitted.
Universal humbled arrival at the trumpet is only distant local context for submission.
Fear of punishment does not address hearing, signs, or guidance.
The blinding of answers on Judgment Day is only a distant use of blindness imagery.
Pharaoh's preserved body as a sign contrasts with people's heedlessness of signs.
Entry in peace does not explain the focus's guidance or reception.
Those arrogant toward God's signs neither believe them nor take the path of right guidance.
The nearby charge that people lacked certainty in God's signs sharpens the focus's believers.
Asks what message they will believe after this, directly extending rejection of revelation.
The father's threat against Abraham concerns idolatry, not responsive hearing.
Moses' call at the fire supplies no material connection to the focus.
The merciful greeting of peace is unrelated to blindness or guidance.
Turning away from their reminder gives a general counterpart to receptive hearing.
Pharaoh's late claim of faith and submission contrasts with timely receptive belief.
Those who hear the Book recognize it as guidance to truth and a straight path.
Demanding a sign from a messenger is only a secondary contrast to believing God's signs.
The Lord's judgment among disputants is nearby context but not the focus's reception claim.
Faith in God and the Last Day with righteous action describes a positive believing response.
The distinction between faith and doubt in the Hereafter is relevant but indirect.
The creation-and-provision challenge does not clarify the hearing or blindness motif.
Divine hearing and knowledge in provision are a different use of hearing.
Directly says the deaf do not hear the call when they are warned by revelation.
Rescue of the distressed and scant remembrance do not explain the focus.
Its command to listen and statement about unguided rebels offer only a procedural parallel.
Calling the messenger merely human and a liar does not directly develop the focus.
God's guidance to His light provides an indirect counterpart to blindness and being guided.
Compelled submission at judgment contrasts with the voluntary submission of believing hearers.
The refusal to believe a messenger presents the opposite response to 27:81.
Immediate judgment question rebukes denial of signs without encompassing them in knowledge.
Requires that an ignorant seeker hear God's words before being returned to safety.
Warning or not warning is equal for people who will not believe, clarifying unreceptive refusal.
God alone guides through darkness, a nearby divine-guidance counterpart to the focus.
Revelation and prophethood provide guidance, yet only some become guided.
Listeners remain veiled from understanding and refuse every sign, directly explaining failed hearing.
The death-punishment scene does not develop guidance, signs, or receptive hearing.
The magicians believe in their Lord's signs and ask to die submitted.
Acknowledges that criminals led them astray, supplying a general error counterpart.
Immediate consequence of wrongdoing and silence follows the surrounding denial of signs.
God's hearing and knowledge do not clarify the human hearing at issue.
A messenger remains commanded to be submitted despite his audience turning away.
Calls revelation insight, guidance, and mercy for a people of certainty.
Contrasts submitted people with criminals, though it does not address signs or hearing.
Commands continued faith in God, messenger, and scripture, with disbelief ending in far error.
Denial of punishment does not clarify the focus's receptive-believer distinction.
A community that guides by truth gives a broad positive counterpart to guidance.
Exposes verbal faith without inward belief and distorted listening, qualifying genuine reception.
The magicians' immediate belief despite Pharaoh's objection illustrates a decisive response.
Hypocritical claims of belief give only an indirect contrast to sincere believing hearers.
The magicians' confession of faith in the Lord of the worlds exemplifies belief after a sign.
Sealed hearts, hearing, and sight provide a foundational account of unreceptive refusal.
The deaf, dumb, and blind neither return nor respond to guidance.
The image of people who hear only a call while deaf, dumb, and blind closely explains failed reception.
Submission is identified with being rightly guided, while the messenger's remaining task is only conveyance.
Clear insights make seeing beneficial and blindness self-destructive, while the messenger is not their guardian.
Divine guidance opens the breast to Islam, directly linking guidance and submission.
Those called to guidance neither follow it nor truly see, directly paralleling the focus's blind error.
Warns against turning away after hearing, exposing merely claimed reception.
Directly rebukes those who say they hear while they do not hear.
Names the deaf and dumb who do not reason as the worst creatures, clarifying spiritual deafness.
Even granted hearing, people lacking inward good would turn away; this closely marks the limit of hearing.
Explicitly rejects the messenger's ability to compel all people into belief.
States that belief occurs only by God's permission, sharpening the limit on human guidance.
No prophet can compel a people to accept a message they dislike.
The prophet's eagerness cannot make most people become believers.
Contrasts blind and seeing, darkness and light, within the question of true guidance.
Sealed hearts, hearing, and sight explain why people do not receive guidance.
A hidden barrier and covered hearts block reception of Qur'anic recitation.
Covers over hearts and deafness in ears cause people to turn away from the Qur'an.
Blindness in this life becomes a more grievous blindness in the Hereafter.
Turning from recalled signs and deaf ears form a direct account of persistent non-guidance.
Turning from remembrance ends in a constricted life and resurrection in blindness.
The blind resurrection is explained by having ignored God's signs while sighted.
Locates true blindness in hearts rather than eyes and calls for hearing hearts.
Questions whether most people truly hear or reason, then calls them more astray than cattle.
Explicitly denies that the messenger can guide whomever he loves; God knows the guided.
Near-verbatim parallel: the messenger cannot make the dead or turning deaf hear the call.
A hearer turns away arrogantly as though he had not heard, dramatizing rejection of signs.
Barriers before, behind, and over the eyes leave the rejecters unable to see.
The Qur'an warns the living and establishes the word against disbelievers, matching the receptive distinction.
An opened breast for Islam contrasts with hardened hearts unreceptive to God's remembrance.
God's message moves receptive skins and hearts, supplying the positive dynamics of hearing revelation.
Those with faith receive guidance and healing, while unbelievers have deafness and blindness.
Whomever God leaves astray has no guiding protector, reinforcing the limit of prophetic agency.
The revealed spirit guides to a straight path, defining the content of guidance offered.
Following desire results in a seal over hearing and heart and a cover over sight.
Some listen to the prophet without understanding; their hearts are sealed and they follow desire.
Those who sever guidance are cursed, deafened, and blinded.
God increases guidance in those already guided, supplying the reciprocal positive side.
The prophet is not a compeller; he can only remind those who heed the warning.
The Qur'an made easy for remembrance highlights the available message against continued refusal.
When people deviated, God let their hearts deviate, linking refusal and misguidance.
Professed faith followed by disbelief seals hearts and prevents understanding.
The condemned admit that listening and reasoning would have kept them from the Fire.
Persistent refusal is depicted by fingers in ears, covered heads, and arrogant persistence.
The shown way divides people into grateful and ungrateful responders.
The command to remind, when reminder benefits, frames the receptive limit of proclamation.
One who fears will remember, providing the positive counterpart to hearing.
The most wretched avoid the reminder, providing the negative counterpart to hearing.
The prophet's role is only to remind, not to create acceptance.
The prophet is not a controller over the hearers, directly limiting his agency.
No compulsion in religion sets the governing boundary against forcing belief or guidance.
God brings believers from darkness into light, the positive counterpart to blindness and error.
Holding fast to God is described as being guided to a straight path.
By the revelation God guides those seeking His pleasure to paths of peace and out of darkness.
If people turn away, the messenger's duty remains clear conveyance rather than control of response.
Hearts and sights are turned away because they first refused belief in the signs.
Even multiplied signs would not make persistent rejecters believe apart from God's will.
The living person given light to walk among people contrasts directly with one in inescapable darkness.
One group is guided while another rightly bears error after taking devils as allies.
Those who deny God's signs and are arrogant toward them supply the opposite response to 27:81.
Whomever God guides is truly guided, while those He leaves astray are the losers.
Whomever God leaves astray has no guide, directly defining the boundary of guidance.
Believers are commanded to respond when God and the messenger call them to what gives life.
Repeated forgiveness requests cannot change the settled refusal of those who disbelieve.
The question of who guides to truth contrasts divine guidance with those who cannot guide unless guided.
A prophet's counsel cannot benefit a people when God wills their error.
God guides to Himself those who turn back, supplying the positive response-side of guidance.
The Book brings people from darkness into light by their Lord's permission.
God's messengers clarify in their people's language, yet guidance and error remain under God's will.
Each community receives a messenger calling for worship of God, but some are guided and some enter error.
Even the prophet's desire for their guidance cannot guide those God leaves astray.
Turning away leaves the messenger only the duty of clear delivery.
God guides whom He wills and leaves astray whom He wills, while holding people accountable for their deeds.
The Qur'an guides to what is most upright and gives good news to believers who act rightly.
Whoever God guides is guided, and those He lets stray have no protectors besides Him.
Whomever God guides is guided, and whomever He leaves astray has no guiding protector.
Following divine guidance prevents going astray or falling into misery.
The messenger calls people to a straight path, defining the guidance he offers.
Clear signs are sent down and God guides whom He wills to a straight path.
Believers answer God's and the messenger's call with “we hear and obey,” the clearest positive counterpart.
Obeying the messenger brings guidance, while his responsibility remains only clear delivery.
Those who strive for God are guided to His ways, presenting responsive movement toward guidance.
Leaders guide by God's command when people are patient and certain of His signs.
Those given knowledge recognize the revelation as truth that guides to the Mighty, Praiseworthy path.
A person whose evil deed is made attractive illustrates how error can appear as guidance.
The decisive word against many leaves them unable to believe, immediately framing 36:10's warning.
Yokes and barriers leave the rejecters unable to see, directly continuing the blindness motif.
Whomever God guides has no misleader, affirming divine supremacy over error.
Whomever God leaves astray has no guide, in a warning of turning away.
God chooses and guides to Himself those who turn back, defining the responsive path.
Turning from the Merciful's reminder brings a companion who steers the person away.
Those companions obstruct the path while their followers think themselves guided.
Whoever does not answer God's caller is neither beyond God nor protected from error.
God sent His messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, identifying the message's purpose.
Clear signs are sent down to bring people from darkness into light.
Those charged with the Torah but not carrying it illustrate unreceptive possession of revelation.
Faith in God is followed by God guiding the believer's heart.
The submitted seek right guidance, while the unjust choose another course.
The Fire's account is made a test so believers increase in faith and doubters are exposed.
Guidance belongs to God, grounding the focus's limit on human direction.
God finding the messenger seeking and then guiding him affirms divine initiative in guidance.
